readerTitle: The 15-minute Friday meeting that keeps a cleaning crew getting better
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 업체, 회계·기장 대행 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 개선은 문제가 터졌을 때 하는 큰 프로젝트가 아니라, 일하는 사람이 매주 작은 불편 하나를 고치고 확인하는 습관이다.
misconception: 개선하려면 큰 개편, 새 시스템, 외부 전문가가 필요하다. 작은 수정은 티가 나지 않아 의미가 없다.

sources.text: Imai, M. (1986). Kaizen: The Key to Japan's Competitive Success. McGraw-Hill.
운영관리의 표준 개념 (지속적 개선, 개선 사이클)
모든 업체와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 청소 업체 계산: 수정 3개로 집 한 곳당 5분 + 4분 + 3분 = 12분 절약. 하루 4곳 × 12분 = 48분, 주 5일 × 48분 = 240분 = 4시간. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
'kaizen'은 일본어로 '개선, 더 나은 방향으로의 변화'라는 뜻으로 설명했습니다. 게시 전 표현을 다시 확인하세요. Imai(1986) 책이 이 용어를 서구에 널리 알렸다는 점은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
소프트웨어 팀의 회고(retrospective)는 애자일 개발에서 흔한 관행으로 일반적으로만 설명했습니다. 특정 수치나 출처는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The 15-minute Friday meeting that keeps a cleaning crew getting better
body: Every Friday at 4 p.m., a three-person house-cleaning crew sits in their van with coffee and answers one question: *what slowed us down this week?*
They pick one answer and fix it before Monday. No consultants, no new software. A year later, they finish the same homes noticeably faster and get fewer complaints.

image.label: Cleaning crew talking in a parked van with a notepad
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 오후 햇살 속에 주차된 밴 안에서 청소 직원 세 명이 커피를 들고 메모장 한 장을 보며 이야기하는 장면. 메모장에는 "What slowed us down?" 한 줄과 체크 표시 하나. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Jobs are running long and complaints are creeping up.
body: You run a small home-cleaning business with two crews. Nothing is broken, but jobs take longer than booked, and clients mention small misses: a skipped mirror, a late arrival.
What do you do first?

options.text: Plan a full overhaul next quarter: new booking software and retraining for everyone
options.feedback: A big change might help, but it costs months and money before you learn anything. Meanwhile the small problems keep repeating every day.

options.text: Hold a short weekly crew huddle, fix one small annoyance at a time, and check if it helped
options.feedback: Cheap, fast and led by the people who see the problems. Each fix is small, but they add up week after week.

options.text: Hire a supervisor to inspect every finished home
options.feedback: You'd catch more misses before clients do. But inspection adds cost and finds problems after they happen, without removing why they happen.

cards.title: Three small fixes, one month.
body: Twelve minutes per home sounds minor. At four homes a day, that's 48 minutes. Over a five-day week, it's **4 hours** of crew time back, nearly room for another booking.

breakdown.label: Pre-packed supply caddies
breakdown.detail: No more hunting in the van for the right spray

breakdown.label: Entry notes in each booking
breakdown.detail: Key, alarm and pet details in one place

breakdown.label: Room-by-room checklist
breakdown.detail: Fewer missed mirrors, fewer return visits

breakdown.label: Saved per home
breakdown.detail: Found by the crew, not a consultant

cards.title: Continuous improvement
body: **Continuous improvement** means making many small changes, often, led by the people who do the work, and checking whether each one helped.
It runs as a loop: notice a problem, try a small fix, check the result, then keep it or drop it. The Japanese word *kaizen*, meaning change for the better, is often used for this idea.

image.label: A loop: notice, try, check, keep
image.brief: 원형 순환 다이어그램. 네 단계 "Notice a problem" → "Try a small fix" → "Check the result" → "Keep or drop" 가 화살표로 이어지고 다시 처음으로 돌아감. 가운데에 작은 계단 아이콘으로 한 바퀴마다 조금씩 올라가는 느낌을 표현.

cards.title: Small, frequent and close to the work.
body: Small changes are cheap and easy to undo, so people are willing to try more of them. A failed experiment costs a week, not a quarter.
The people doing the work see problems managers miss. The crew knows exactly where the minutes go.
And fixes stack. Once a fix works, it becomes the new normal way of doing the job. Next week's improvement starts from a better place.

cards.title: It works alongside big changes, not instead of them.
body: Sometimes you need a big step: a new location, new equipment, a new system. Small fixes can't replace that.

But big changes rarely work perfectly on day one. Continuous improvement is how a new system gets good after launch. Teams inside larger companies use the same loop, from a finance team's month-end to a warehouse shift.
cards.softwareNote: Many software teams build this in as a *retrospective*: at the end of each work cycle, they ask what slowed them down and pick one thing to change next cycle.

cards.title: The habit dies easily.
body: It fails when ideas go into a box and nobody answers. People stop speaking up within weeks.
It fails when people fear blame. Problems get hidden instead of named.
It costs real time. Fifteen minutes a week is a small price, but it must be protected.
And polishing has limits. If the whole process is wrong, ten small fixes won't save it. That's when you need a bigger change.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: Your firm closes the books for 40 small-business clients every month. The month-end close is always a few days late. Your staff have plenty of ideas about why.
How do you start improving it?

options.text: Run a big staff survey once a year and act on the top ideas
options.feedback: You'll hear good ideas, but only once a year. Twelve late month-ends pass before anything changes.

options.text: After each close, hold a 20-minute review, fix the one delay that hurt most, and compare next month
options.feedback: A fix every month, tested by the next close. You learn which changes actually help.

options.text: Collect every idea and put them all in place next month
options.feedback: Lots of change at once can overwhelm the team. Even if things improve, you won't know which change did it.

cards.title: Better is a weekly habit, not a one-time project.
body: Small fixes, made often by the people closest to the work, add up to more than most big overhauls.
**Try it today:** ask your team one question: what slowed us down this week? Pick one answer, fix it, and check again in seven days.
